Chapter IV.

Catherine had not heard from her sister in three weeks, and she began to fear that something was amiss. She was, therefore, much relieved when at last the post brought her two letters in succession.

Dear Catherine,

I write to you in haste, for I have only a few minutes before the carriage is brought round. The journey has been more tedious than I had imagined, and I am quite worn down by the constant rattling of the wheels and the dust of the road. Mrs. Allen, whom you remember from Bath, sends her regards, and hopes that your mother is in better health since last we spoke.

The country here is exceedingly beautiful, with hills and small woods on every side, and the most delightful village church I have ever seen. I shall write again from London, and tell you everything.

Yours ever,
Isabella

Some days later a second letter arrived, this one in a hand Catherine did not at first recognize.

My dear Miss Morland,

I take the liberty of writing on a matter of some delicacy, the particulars of which I would prefer not to commit to paper. If you can contrive to call upon me at your earliest convenience, you will oblige me very much, and you will, I think, be glad you came.

Sincerely yours,
Eleanor Tilney
